decision_nodes.title: Sodium Bicarbonate Drip Protocol
decision_nodes.body:
[Bicarbonate Drip Steps](#/info/bicarbdrip-steps)

This consult is for continuous sodium bicarbonate infusion, not reflex ampules during routine resuscitation.

Common ED/ICU indications:
- Severe metabolic acidemia, especially pH <=7.20 with moderate-severe AKI or bicarbonate loss
- Hyperkalemia with metabolic acidosis when isotonic bicarbonate can be used as resuscitative fluid
- Salicylate toxicity requiring serum/urine alkalinization
- Sodium-channel blocker toxicity after bolus therapy when QRS/pH targets require maintenance infusion

Do not use bicarbonate drip as routine treatment for cardiac arrest, isolated lactic acidosis without severe acidemia/AKI, routine DKA, or primary respiratory acidosis.
decision_nodes.summary: Bicarbonate infusion is indication-specific; avoid routine use without severe acidemia, alkalinization target, or tox indication.

decision_nodes.title: Indication
decision_nodes.body: Why are you starting a bicarbonate drip?

options.label: Severe metabolic acidemia / AKI
options.description: pH <=7.20, HCO3 low, AKI/uremia or bicarbonate loss physiology

options.label: TCA / sodium-channel blocker
options.description: QRS widening, ventricular dysrhythmia, hypotension after boluses

decision_nodes.summary: The target and rate depend on whether the goal is pH correction, potassium shift, urine alkalinization, or sodium-channel rescue.

decision_nodes.title: Severe Metabolic Acidemia / AKI
decision_nodes.body:
Consider bicarbonate infusion when severe metabolic acidemia is clinically important and reversible/supportable.

Best-supported ICU phenotype:
- pH <=7.20 with low bicarbonate and moderate-severe AKI
- Uremic or non-anion-gap/bicarbonate-loss acidosis
- Severe acidemia contributing to vasopressor resistance or cardiac dysfunction

Recipe:
- [Sodium bicarbonate](#/drug/sodium-bicarbonate/isotonic bicarbonate infusion) 150 mEq in 1 L D5W or sterile water per local pharmacy policy
- Typical rate 100-250 mL/hr, or as resuscitative fluid if volume depleted
- Target pH often >7.20 initially, then >7.30 when using BICAR-ICU-style endpoints

Treat the cause and plan dialysis when acidosis is refractory or due to renal failure/toxin requiring clearance.
decision_nodes.summary: Best evidence is severe acidemia with AKI; bicarbonate is a bridge, not source control.

decision_nodes.title: Hyperkalemia + Metabolic Acidosis
decision_nodes.body:
Bicarbonate is most useful for hyperkalemia when metabolic acidosis is present.

Do first if ECG changes/severe K:
- Calcium for membrane stabilization
- Insulin/dextrose and albuterol for rapid intracellular shift
- Dialysis/diuresis/potassium binders for removal when appropriate

Bicarbonate strategy:
- Use [Sodium bicarbonate](#/drug/sodium-bicarbonate/hyperkalemia with metabolic acidosis) isotonic infusion as resuscitative fluid when hypovolemic/acidotic
- Recipe: 150 mEq in 1 L D5W or sterile water per policy
- Rate: 500-1000 mL/hr initially if true resuscitation fluid is needed; slower if euvolemic or overload risk
- Once serum bicarbonate is >24 and additional volume is needed, transition to balanced crystalloid

Do not rely on bicarbonate alone for life-threatening hyperkalemia.
decision_nodes.summary: Isotonic bicarbonate can help acidotic hyperkalemia, but calcium/insulin/removal remain essential.

decision_nodes.title: Salicylate Toxicity
decision_nodes.body:
Goal is serum and urine alkalinization, not correction of a bicarbonate number.

Initial sequence:
- Call poison center/toxicology and nephrology early
- Give [Sodium bicarbonate](#/drug/sodium-bicarbonate/salicylate toxicity) 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus if severe toxicity, acidemia, altered mental status, or before unavoidable intubation
- Start infusion: 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate in 1 L D5W, typically 150-250 mL/hr
- Add [Potassium chloride IV](#/drug/potassium-chloride-iv/severe hypokalemia) 20-40 mEq/L unless contraindicated; hypokalemia blocks urine alkalinization

Targets:
- Serum pH 7.45-7.55, avoid >7.60
- Urine pH 7.5-8.0
- Urine output 2-3 mL/kg/hr when feasible

Do not use acetazolamide. Escalate to hemodialysis for severe poisoning or alkalinization failure.
decision_nodes.summary: Salicylate bicarbonate infusion targets urine pH and requires aggressive potassium support.

decision_nodes.title: TCA / Sodium-Channel Blocker
decision_nodes.body:
Bicarbonate infusion is maintenance therapy after boluses when sodium-channel blockade persists.

Initial therapy:
- [Sodium bicarbonate](#/drug/sodium-bicarbonate/TCA Overdose — Sodium Channel Blockade) 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus
- Repeat boluses q3-5 min until QRS narrows, hypotension improves, or pH target reached
- Target serum pH 7.50-7.55 and QRS <100 ms when feasible

Infusion:
- 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate in 1 L D5W at 150-250 mL/hr
- Continue while QRS or hemodynamics require alkalinization
- Monitor pH, potassium, ionized calcium, sodium, QRS width

Avoid class IA/IC antiarrhythmics. Treat seizures with benzodiazepines and involve poison center/toxicology.
decision_nodes.summary: TCA/sodium-channel toxicity uses boluses first, then infusion to maintain pH/QRS targets.

decision_nodes.title: Not Routine Bicarbonate Drip
decision_nodes.body:
Do not start bicarbonate infusion for:
- Routine cardiac arrest/CPR without hyperkalemia or sodium-channel blocker toxicity
- Isolated respiratory acidosis; improve ventilation instead
- Routine lactic acidosis without severe acidemia/AKI or bicarbonate-loss physiology
- Routine DKA; insulin/fluids/potassium are definitive, bicarbonate generally only if pH <6.9 by DKA protocols
- Metabolic alkalosis
- Uncontrolled volume overload or severe hypernatremia unless benefit clearly outweighs risk

If pH is critically low, identify whether bicarbonate can be ventilated off as CO2; inadequate ventilation can worsen intracellular/respiratory acidosis.
decision_nodes.recommendation: Hold bicarbonate drip and treat the underlying process unless a clear indication/target exists.
decision_nodes.summary: Bicarbonate infusion should not be reflexive for routine arrest, respiratory acidosis, DKA, or lactic acidosis.

decision_nodes.title: Recipe / Administration
decision_nodes.body:
Common isotonic bicarbonate recipe:
- 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate = three 50 mEq ampules of 8.4% NaHCO3
- Add to 1 L D5W or sterile water per local pharmacy policy
- Final solution is approximately isotonic bicarbonate, ~150 mEq/L sodium bicarbonate

Rates:
- Maintenance/metabolic acidosis: commonly 100-250 mL/hr
- Hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis with hypovolemia: may run 500-1000 mL/hr as resuscitative fluid
- Salicylate or sodium-channel toxicity: commonly 150-250 mL/hr, titrated to pH/urine/QRS targets

Line considerations:
- Use pump and label clearly
- Central access preferred for repeated hypertonic ampules or concentrated preparations
- Peripheral isotonic bicarbonate infusion is commonly used if IV is reliable and local policy allows
decision_nodes.summary: Standard drip recipe is 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate in 1 L D5W/sterile water, rate by indication.

decision_nodes.title: Monitoring
decision_nodes.body:
Core monitoring:
- VBG/ABG q2-4 hr during active titration; q1-2 hr if unstable or target-dependent tox case
- BMP q2-4 hr: sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, creatinine
- Ionized calcium q4-6 hr or sooner if symptomatic/hypocalcemia risk
- Volume status, pulmonary edema, urine output
- Continuous ECG for hyperkalemia, TCA/sodium-channel toxicity, severe acidemia, or rapid shifts

Toxicology targets:
- Salicylate: serum pH 7.45-7.55, urine pH 7.5-8.0, K often >=4.0-4.5
- TCA/sodium-channel blocker: QRS narrowing and serum pH 7.50-7.55

Ventilation requirement:
- Bicarbonate generates CO2. Ensure the patient can increase minute ventilation or is mechanically ventilated appropriately.
decision_nodes.summary: Monitor pH, sodium, potassium, ionized calcium, volume, ECG, and ventilation.

decision_nodes.title: Complications
decision_nodes.body:
Watch for:
- Hypernatremia and hyperosmolality
- Hypokalemia from intracellular shift
- Lower ionized calcium with tetany, seizures, hypotension, or reduced contractility
- Volume overload/pulmonary edema
- Metabolic alkalosis
- Increased CO2 load with worsening respiratory acidosis if ventilation is inadequate
- Delayed dialysis when bicarbonate is used beyond its role as a bridge

Stop or slow the drip when targets are reached, adverse effects develop, or definitive therapy has taken over.
decision_nodes.summary: Major risks are sodium/volume load, hypokalemia, low ionized calcium, alkalemia, and CO2 generation.

decision_nodes.title: Disposition / Handoff
decision_nodes.body:
Most bicarbonate drip patients need ICU, stepdown, or close monitored care.

Handoff must include:
- Indication and target: pH, urine pH, QRS, potassium, or bridge to dialysis
- Recipe and current rate
- Total bicarbonate/sodium administered
- Latest pH, Na, K, ionized Ca, creatinine, urine output
- Ventilation status and CO2 clearance
- Stop criteria and next lab time
- Toxicology/nephrology/poison center recommendations when applicable
decision_nodes.recommendation: Continue only with a clear endpoint, monitoring schedule, and definitive treatment plan.
decision_nodes.summary: Bicarbonate drips require monitored disposition and explicit stop criteria.
